title: From C to a running program
subtitle: Compilers, linkers, executables and libraries: MS-DOS 4.00 vs FreeBSD 15.1

slides.title: From source text to a process
slides.subtitle: Preprocess, compile, assemble, link, load: on both systems

slides.title: Five stages, five kinds of file
bullets: Preprocess: #include and #define expanded, comments gone (CL /P, cc -E)
Compile: C to instructions for one CPU and one calling convention
Assemble: bytes + names defined + names needed + relocations = object file
Link: combine objects and library members, fix addresses, write the executable
Load: copy or map it, finish relocation, jump to the entry point
FreeBSD adds a sixth step: the run-time linker attaches shared libraries
slides.notes: Define the vocabulary first: translation unit, object file, relocation (Microsoft says fixup), executable, library, loader. Every later slide is one of these stages seen in a real file. Stress that both systems were built with exactly these tools: MS C 5.10 and LINK 3.65 are in v4.0/src/TOOLS, and every FreeBSD 15.1 binary names clang 19.1.7 and LLD 19.1.7 in its .comment section.

slides.title: The pipeline on both systems
slides.caption: MS C 5.10 writes OMF directly from pass 3; clang has an integrated assembler. Only FreeBSD links at run time.
slides.notes: Walk left to right on both lanes. The striking point on MS-DOS is that there is no assembler run: C3 writes the object file. On FreeBSD the program file only names libc.so.7; the run-time linker brings in libc and libsys when the program starts.

slides.title: How MS-DOS 4.00 compiles its own C programs
callouts: FDISK, MEM, ATTRIB, REPLACE ... are C
slides.notes: The build counted bytes. Small model, size optimization, packed structs. The kernel, IO.SYS and COMMAND.COM are assembly; about a dozen utilities are C. MEM.EXE has the same C run-time segments as the students' HELLO.EXE.

slides.title: Lab 5.1: CL runs three passes (CL /Bd)
slides.text:
CL /Bd /c HELLO.C
P1 : ` T:\c1.exe -il 014595 -f HELLO.C ... -A snd -Ze -DM_I86 -DMSDOS
       -DM_I86SM -DM_I8086 -I T:/BLD/INC -W 1  '
P2 : ` T:\c2.exe -il 014595 -ef T:\c23.err -Oc -Ot -G0 -A snd -W 1  '
P3 : ` T:\c3.exe -il 014595 ... -FPi -Ot -c HELLO.OBJ -A snd -CC 0sO  '

C1: preprocess + parse     C2: optimize, generate code     C3: write OMF
No MASM pass.  /B1 T:\C1L.EXE swaps pass 1: same object, byte for byte.
slides.notes: Real output, abridged. /Bd is not in CL.HLP; we found it in the strings of CL.EXE. It plays the role of cc -### on FreeBSD. In the lab, students run CL /P, CL /c /Fc and LINK /MAP and read every intermediate file: HELLO.I, HELLO.COD, HELLO.OBJ, HELLO.MAP, then run HELLO.EXE on MS-DOS 4.00.

slides.title: One line of C, two compilers: abs()

left.heading: MS-DOS 4.00: MS C 5.10 /Ox
bullets: Argument on the stack: [bp+4]
cmp, jge, neg: two return paths
No conditional move on the 8086
/Ox drops the __chkstk call
_myabs: names get an underscore

right.heading: FreeBSD 15.1: clang 19 -O2
bullets: Argument in a register: %edi
mov, neg, cmovs: no branch
Result in %eax, 7 instructions
Real code from /lib/libc.so.7
abs: no underscore

slides.notes: Outputs 5.7 and 5.8. The source is the same line, return(j < 0 ? -j : j). The differences are the calling convention (stack versus registers), the instruction set (cmovs exists only from the Pentium Pro), and the optimizer. Ask the class to count bytes: 21 for MS C, 13 for clang.

slides.title: Memory models: near and far
slides.caption: A near pointer is a 16-bit offset; a far pointer is segment:offset. 64-bit FreeBSD has only code models.
slides.notes: The 8086 reaches 64 KB per segment register. Memory models decide which pointers and calls are near. DS = SS = DGROUP in every model, which is why a near pointer can point at globals and at locals. On amd64 the small code model keeps code and static data within 2 GB so that RIP-relative 32-bit displacements work.

slides.title: Lab 5.2: the same function, /AS and /AL
slides.text:
/AS small                         /AL large
_sum PROC NEAR                    _sum PROC FAR
mov si,[bp+4]       8b 76 04      les si,[bp+6]         c4 76 06
mov ax,[bx][si]     8b 00         mov ax,es:[bx][si]    26 8b 00
ret                 c3            retf                  cb
call _sum           e8 ba ff      push ds / push cs / call _sum
call _printf        e8 00 00      call FAR PTR _printf  9a 00 00 00 00

MODS.EXE 7,301 bytes, 4 relocations    MODL.EXE 10,033 bytes, 70 relocations
slides.notes: Real .COD output, condensed (Output 5.10). Arguments move up by 2 because the return address is 4 bytes. Every far call holds a segment value, so every far call becomes a relocation in the .EXE: 3 in the user module, 55 in the library code, 12 in library data. push cs plus a near call fakes a far call to a function in the same segment.

slides.title: Object files, linking and start-up
slides.subtitle: OMF records and ELF sections; crt0 and crt1

slides.title: What an object file must say
slides.notes: The same six kinds of information in two encodings. OMF is a stream of records with names numbered by order of appearance; ELF is a set of tables. The frame in an OMF fixup has no ELF counterpart: it exists because 8086 addresses are relative to a segment register.

slides.title: Lab 5.3: reading HELLO.OBJ with omfdump.py
bullets: COMENT 9Fh 'SLIBCE': the library name travels inside the object
EXTDEF __acrtused, _printf; COMDEF _table (200 bytes); PUBDEF _main
Fixup +017h: target _DATA, frame DGROUP: LINK stores 42h, not 0
call _square needs no fixup; call _printf does
CL /Zl removes the library comment: LINK fails with L2029
slides.notes: Run omfdump live and match each fixup offset with an instruction in HELLO.COD. The frame/target distinction is the hard part: draw DGROUP, _DATA and _counter on a line. Then dump SLIBCE.LIB --member "dos\crt0.asm" to show where __acrtused (absolute 9876h), the STACK segment and the start address come from.

slides.title: FreeBSD's entry point: _start
slides.code:
_start:
⋮
        pushq   %rbp                    /* Align stack, terminate call chain. */
⋮
        movq    %rsp, %rbp
⋮
        movq    %rsi, %rcx              /* cleanup */
        movslq  (%rdi), %rax            /* long *ap; tmpargc = *ap */
        leaq    0x8(%rdi), %rsi         /* argv = ap + 1 */
        leaq    0x10(%rdi, %rax, 8), %rdx /* env = ap + 2 + tmpargc */
        movl    %eax, %edi              /* argc = tmpargc */
⋮
        /* __libc_start1(argc, argv, env, cleanup, main) */
        callq   __libc_start1
callouts: argc, argv, env from the initial stack
slides.notes: crt1.o is FreeBSD's crt0. The kernel or the run-time linker leaves argc, argv, NULL, envp, NULL on the stack; _start turns that into C arguments. __libc_start1 in libc registers cleanup with atexit, runs static initializers in static programs, sets errno to 0 and calls exit(main(...)).

slides.title: Before main: crt0 and crt1

left.heading: MS-DOS 4.00: __astart (crt0)
bullets: INT 21h AH=30h: refuse DOS 1.x
SS = DS = DGROUP, set SP
AH=4Ah: give back unused memory
Clear BSS with REP STOSB
Build argv, environ; call _main
exit: flush, __nullcheck, AH=4Ch

right.heading: FreeBSD 15.1: _start (crt1.o)
bullets: Kernel built the stack and auxv
Run-time linker ran the initializers
Kernel zero-fills BSS pages
__libc_start1: environ, __progname
errno = 0; exit(main(...))
atexit(cleanup) from ld-elf.so.1

slides.notes: The jobs that crt0 must do itself (switch stack, shrink the memory block, clear BSS) are done by the kernel on FreeBSD. __nullcheck is a fun detail: it XORs the 42h bytes at DS:0 and prints R6001 null pointer assignment, changing exit code 0 to 255.

slides.title: Executable files and libraries
slides.subtitle: .COM, MZ, ELF; static and shared libraries

slides.title: Three executable formats
slides.caption: .COM: a memory image. MZ: header, relocation table, image. ELF: program headers the kernel maps.
slides.notes: EXEC decides .COM or .EXE by the first two bytes, not by the name. ELF segments are what the kernel maps; sections are for linkers and debuggers. FileSiz smaller than MemSiz in the last LOAD is BSS, the counterpart of e_minalloc (in ls's third LOAD the excess is only .relro_padding).

slides.title: The MZ header in EXE.INC
slides.code:
EXE_file    STRUC
exe_signature   DW  ?                   ; must contain 4D5A  (yay zibo!)
exe_len_mod_512 DW  ?                   ; low 9 bits of length
exe_pages       DW  ?                   ; number of 512b pages in file
exe_rle_count   DW  ?                   ; count of reloc entries
exe_par_dir     DW  ?                   ; number of paragraphs before image
exe_min_BSS     DW  ?                   ; minimum number of para of BSS
exe_max_BSS     DW  ?                   ; max number of para of BSS
exe_SS          DW  ?                   ; stack of image
exe_SP          DW  ?                   ; SP of image
exe_chksum      DW  ?                   ; checksum  of file (ignored)
exe_IP          DW  ?                   ; IP of entry
exe_CS          DW  ?                   ; CS of entry
exe_rle_table   DW  ?                   ; byte offset of reloc table
exe_iov         DW  ?                   ; overlay number (0 for root)
exe_sym_tab     DD  ?                   ; offset of symbol table in file
EXE_file    ENDS
callouts: SS:SP and CS:IP relative to the image
slides.notes: Every field can be checked against HELLO.MAP: CS:IP = 0000:0040 is __astart, SS:SP = 0216:0800 is the end of STACK. e_minalloc is the BSS and stack that are not in the file; e_maxalloc = FFFFh asks for all memory, which is why crt0 gives memory back.

slides.title: EXEC relocates an .EXE
slides.code:
MOV     SI,exec_rel_fac

exec_reloc_one:
        OR      DX,DX                   ; Any more entries?
        JE      exec_set_PDBJ

exec_get_addr:
        LDS     BX,DWORD PTR ES:[DI]    ; Get ra/sa of entry
        MOV     AX,DS                   ; Relocate address of item
        ADD     AX,SI
        MOV     DS,AX
        ADD     [BX],SI
        ADD     DI,4
        DEC     DX
        LOOP    exec_reloc_one          ; End of internal buffer?
callouts: No names, no types: one kind
slides.notes: This is the entire relocation step of MS-DOS: add the load segment to every listed word. In SEGS.EXE the 4 words hold 0173h, DGROUP's paragraph; on our DOS they became 1387h (load segment 1214h). Offsets never change. The EXEPACK unpacker and CONVERT's stub contain copies of this loop.

slides.title: Lab 5.4: numbers from the real MS-DOS 4.00

stats.label: bytes: largest .COM that MS-DOS 4.00 EXEC runs
bytes: HELLOC.COM made by EXE2BIN from an 821-byte .EXE
MS-DOS 4.00 .COM files that are .EXEs wrapped by CONVERT
bytes SORT.EXE is shorter than its header says

slides.notes: All measured in the lab. 65,280 bytes gives Program too big to fit in memory: EXEC asks for FF00h bytes and treats a full read as no memory (EXEC.ASM lines 597-598). EXE2BIN refuses SEGREF (one fixup) and HELLO.EXE (a stack segment). BACKUP.COM starts with a JMP, the word Converted and a complete MZ header.

slides.title: Lab 5.5: a static library with LIB
bullets: LIB MYLIB +ADDUP +TIMES; builds a 2-member library
LINK /MAP USELIB,,,MYLIB; pulls ADDUP only: _times is not in the map
Without the library: L2029 Unresolved externals: _addup
Two objects defining _addup: L2025 symbol defined more than once
Same rules for ar and .a files on FreeBSD
slides.notes: Members are linked whole, only when they define a name that is still undefined; object files named on the command line are always linked. That is why the C library has one function per module: printf.c is 60 bytes and calls __output, which is 2,267 bytes.

slides.title: Lab 5.6: an ELF object (nasm -f elf64 bump.asm)
slides.text:
readelf -r bump.o
Offset  Type            Symbol + Addend
0x02    R_X86_64_PC32   counter - 4     mov 0x0(%rip),%eax
0x08    R_X86_64_PC32   .data - 4       add 0x0(%rip),%eax
0x0e    R_X86_64_PC32   counter - 4     mov %eax,0x0(%rip)
0x15    R_X86_64_PLT32  report - 4      jmp report

PC32: S + A - P.  A = -4: the CPU adds to the next instruction's address.
crt1.o: R_X86_64_64 main (movabs), R_X86_64_PLT32 __libc_start1
slides.notes: Real output, condensed. Even a reference to a variable in the same file (step in .data) needs a relocation, because .data has no address yet. Compare with the OMF self-relative fixup: same arithmetic. Ask students to compute the bytes for a given S and P.

slides.title: Lab 5.7: FreeBSD 15.1 binaries, read with readelf
slides.notes: Real static facts from base.txz, confirmed in the course VM. 189 of the 191 ELF programs in /bin and /sbin are PIEs; init is static so that the first process does not depend on shared libraries, and /sbin/nologin is a symlink to a static /usr/sbin/nologin. In the VM, readelf, objdump and nm are the LLVM tools: same facts, slightly different layout. libsys.so.7 is new in FreeBSD 15: the system call stubs moved there; libc's write calls __sys_write through an interposing table.

slides.title: Static and dynamic linking
slides.caption: MS-DOS copies library code into every .EXE; FreeBSD records NEEDED and binds at run time.
slides.notes: On MS-DOS the only shared code is the OS itself, reached by INT 21h. On FreeBSD a few hundred programs share one libc.so.7, on disk and in memory, because code pages are mapped from the same file and never written.

slides.title: Lazy binding: the first call
callouts: PLT -> GOT slot -> back into the PLT
Look the symbol up by name
Store it in the GOT slot: later calls go direct
slides.notes: In /bin/ls the GOT slot of __libc_start1 initially holds 0x8506, the push instruction in its own PLT entry. GOT[1] and GOT[2] are filled by init_pltgot with the object and _rtld_bind_start. LD_BIND_NOW binds everything at start-up instead.

slides.title: From exec to main
slides.caption: EXEC does everything inside one INT 21h call; execve maps and starts ld-elf.so.1, which loads, relocates and jumps.
slides.notes: The kernel sets the entry point to the interpreter's and passes AT_PHDR, AT_ENTRY and AT_BASE in the auxiliary vector. _rtld relocates itself, loads NEEDED objects breadth-first, relocates, runs initializers and returns the program's entry. ldd stops it right after loading: LD_TRACE_LOADED_OBJECTS.

slides.title: Lab 5.8: the FreeBSD toolchain at work (VM)
bullets: cc -###: in-process clang -cc1, then ld with crt1.o, crtbegin.o, -lc
No PIE unless asked: hello is EXEC at 0x200000
ldd and LD_TRACE_LOADED_OBJECTS: libc, libsys, [vdso]
truss: libmap.conf, hints, open + mmap per library, then write
Sizes: hello 9,832; hello-static 4,402,664; HELLO.EXE 7,271
slides.notes: Outputs 5.40-5.45, captured in the course VM. Ask which file in the cc -### command plays the role of crt0 (crt1.o, not Scrt1.o: no PIE by default; the base system adds -fPIE -pie in bsd.prog.mk), and how each linker learns the name of the C library (COMENT 9Fh versus -lc). hello-static is big because of DWARF from libc.a, not code.

slides.title: Study case 5.B: relocation twice
slides.caption: MZ: add the load segment to listed words, in the kernel. ELF: base + addend or symbol lookup, in the process.
slides.notes: SEGS.EXE on our DOS: PSP 1204h, image at 1214h, DGROUP 1387h = 1214h + 173h. In ls, R_X86_64_RELATIVE writes B + 0x1d78 at B + 0x99e0. The GOT exists so that code is never patched and can stay shared.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: The same five stages on both systems; the files they leave are readable
Object files: code + names defined + names needed + relocations
MS-DOS relocates only segment values, once, inside EXEC
FreeBSD resolves names at run time: NEEDED, PLT, GOT, ld-elf.so.1
Memory models existed because of 64 KB segments; amd64 has code models
No shared libraries on MS-DOS: INT 21h and INT 2Fh played that role
slides.notes: Close with the comparison tables of sections 5.6 and 5.8. The design difference is where names are resolved: before the file exists (MS-DOS) or when the process starts (FreeBSD).
